title: JSX Basics
description: Learn JSX syntax, expressions, and how it differs from HTML.

data.text: **JSX** (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you write HTML-like code inside your JavaScript files. It is the template language of React and compiles down to `React.createElement` calls.

JSX is not a separate language or template engine. It is valid JavaScript that your build tool (Vite, webpack, etc.) transforms into function calls. The result is the same DOM you would create manually, but with much less code.

data.title: JSX vs createElement

data.text: Wrap any JavaScript expression in curly braces `{}` inside JSX. This includes variables, function calls, math, and ternary operators.

data.title: Embedding Expressions

data.text: JSX looks like HTML but follows JavaScript naming rules. This is the most common source of confusion for beginners.

rows: class is a reserved word in JavaScript
for is a reserved word in JavaScript
Style is an object in JSX

data.title: JSX Style Object

data.text: JSX expressions must return a single parent element. Use a `<div>` or a **React Fragment** (`<></>`) to wrap multiple sibling elements without adding extra nodes to the DOM.

data.title: Wrapping with Fragment
data.content: Using Fragments to avoid extra DOM nodes

data.title: Common Mistake
data.text: Returning multiple elements without a parent wrapper is a syntax error. Always wrap siblings in a single element or Fragment.
Because JSX is JavaScript, you can use any JavaScript feature inside curly braces: arrays, objects, functions, and even other JSX.

data.title: Objects and Arrays in JSX

terms.definition: JavaScript XML — a syntax extension for writing HTML-like markup inside JavaScript.
A lightweight wrapper (<></>) that groups children without adding DOM nodes.
Any valid JavaScript unit (variable, function call, operation) wrapped in {}.
Naming convention where words are joined without spaces and each starts with a capital letter (onClick, className).

data.title: Exercise: Write Valid JSX
data.description: Practice writing JSX with correct syntax and embedded expressions.
steps: Create a ProfileCard component in App.jsx.
Use a Fragment to wrap an h2 and a p tag.
Embed a name variable and a boolean isActive inside the JSX.
Use className instead of class and onClick instead of onclick.
data.expectedOutcome: A valid JSX component that renders a profile card with dynamic values.

items.question: Is JSX required in React?
items.answer: No. You can use React.createElement directly, but JSX is the standard because it is more readable and concise.

items.question: Can I use JSX with other libraries?
items.answer: Yes. While designed for React, JSX can compile to other target functions (e.g., Preact, Solid).

items.question: Why does React use className instead of class?
items.answer: class is a reserved keyword in JavaScript. JSX is JavaScript, not HTML, so it uses className.

items.question: Does JSX run in the browser?
items.answer: No. Browsers do not understand JSX. Build tools like Vite compile JSX into standard JavaScript before serving it.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension for writing UI markup.
Use {} to embed any JavaScript expression inside JSX.
All tags must be closed; use Fragments to avoid extra DOM nodes.
Use camelCase for attributes: className, onClick, htmlFor.
JSX compiles to React.createElement at build time.
data.takeaway: You now know how to read and write valid JSX. Next, you'll build your first real React application.
